cultivar: Menghai large-leaf and other Yunnan assamica plantation and arbor leaf, blended
processing: Raw pu-erh maocha blended to a fixed recipe around grade-4 leaf, with finer buds on the face and coarser leaf inside, steamed and hydraulically pressed into a 357 g 'seven sons' cake; the recipe has been pressed every year since the 1970s.
harvest_season: Blended across seasons and years; sold by production year and batch, not by harvest.
appearance_dry: A tight, even cake with a bud-dusted face, dark-green to brown leaf of mixed grades, the Dayi logo wrapper and a batch number on the box or wrapper.
appearance_liquor: Bright yellow-orange when young, deep amber to red after twenty years, clear.
appearance_wet: Mixed grades of medium leaf with reddish edges and a few stems, opening evenly after the rinse.
taste_profile: The benchmark Menghai cup: a firm bitterness, light smoke in some batches, dried grass and honey, a drying grip when young, and with age plum, wood, camphor and a long warming sweetness.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice; factory cakes are tight. Break along the layers with a pick. Boiling water; young batches want very short steeps, batches over ten years take a clay pot and longer infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and batch number (for example 1801 means 2018, first batch), with the year as the main driver of price: the late-1980s to early-1990s batches known as '88 Qing Bing' are the legendary aged examples, 1990s and early-2000s batches are expensive collector tea, 2003–2012 batches are the classic mid-aged buys, and current batches are cheap and are bought by the tong (seven cakes) to age. In the Chinese market, especially the Guangdong trade, recent 7542 is traded almost like a commodity and prices move with speculation as much as with taste. Storage splits the price for any given batch: dry Kunming stock stays sharp and bright, Guangdong humid stock is darker and softer and is what most people mean by a 'typical' aged 7542.
description:
7542 is the recipe number that defines standard raw pu-erh: a blended cake from the Menghai Tea Factory, now trading as Dayi (TAETEA), pressed to the same formula every year since the recipe was set in 1975. The code reads 75 for the recipe year, 4 for the leaf grade of the blend and 2 for the Menghai factory, and the cake is the one everyone measures other factory sheng against.

The leaf is plantation and arbor maocha from across Menghai County and beyond, blended by grade so that the cake tastes consistent year to year, with finer bud-rich leaf on the face and coarser leaf inside. It is steamed and pressed by machine into a tight 357 g disc, sold in stacks of seven wrapped in bamboo leaf, which is where the 'seven sons cake' name comes from.

Young, a 7542 is bitter, grassy, lightly smoky in some batches and gripping; it is not meant to be drunk young, though plenty of people do. Across ten to twenty years in reasonable storage it becomes plum, wood, camphor and a long warming sweetness, the taste most drinkers mean by aged pu-erh. Brew it with boiling water, two rinses and short steeps while it is young; give it a clay pot and longer infusions once it has gone brown.

It is sold by year and batch, with the batch code on the wrapper or box, and it is the most traded cake in the world: the late-1980s '88 Qing Bing' batches are legendary and priced like fine wine, 1990s and early-2000s batches are serious collector tea, 2003–2012 batches are the sensible way to taste mid-aged factory tea, and current batches are cheap and bought by the tong to put away. The fame brings fakes at every age; buy from established dealers and learn the wrapper, inner ticket and neifei details of the batch you are buying.

If you want one reference cake to calibrate your palate, this is it; drink a current batch next to a ten-year-old one and you will understand what 'Menghai flavour' and 'ageing' mean in a single afternoon.
sources_note: The recipe-number convention (year, grade, factory) and the 1975 date are standard; the '88 Qing Bing' label covers batches from roughly 1988–1992 in trade usage. The English Wikipedia article on the Menghai Tea Factory does not exist, hence the umbrella link.
